docs.text:
PKI and cryptography tools, documentation, and resources.

JKLab is a technology development brand dedicated to researching PKI and cryptographic technologies and creating practical software tools. Leveraging expertise in certificates, digital signatures, encryption, and security protocols, we aim to resolve technical challenges faced by developers and provide efficient development environments. We continuously research and develop PKI development tools and cryptography-related solutions, including our flagship project, BerEditor. By bridging specialized technology with practical tools, JKLab supports the development of security software that is both more convenient and efficient.

Features PKI Technology

PKI (Public Key Infrastructure) is a security framework that utilizes public-key cryptography to verify the identities of users and systems, while ensuring data confidentiality, integrity, authentication, and non-repudiation. It serves as a core foundational technology for internet communication, digital signatures, digital certificate management, and corporate security systems.

BerEditor

BerEditor is an integrated GUI tool designed to support developers working with PKI and cryptographic technologies. It facilitates the development of security protocols and troubleshooting by analyzing and validating ASN.1 encoded data, digital certificates, digital signatures, and various other PKI-related data.

CertMan

CertMan is a certificate management tool that supports the management and verification of digital certificates and Public Key Infrastructure (PKI). It enables users to examine certificate issuance details, validity periods, public keys, extension fields, and certificate chains, while facilitating the efficient execution of technical tasks related to certificate management.

CryptokiMan

CryptokiMan is a tool designed to support the management and development of cryptographic devices and tokens based on the PKCS#11 standard. It interfaces with Hardware Security Modules (HSMs), smart cards, and PKCS#11-compliant cryptographic modules, enabling users to verify and test cryptographic objects, key pairs, cryptographic operations, and digital signature functions.

docs.title: Cryptography, Mathematics, and OpenSSL: A PKI Developer's Perspective
docs.text: Working on public key infrastructure (PKI) often brings me face to face with cryptography and mathematics. Cryptographic algorithms depend on mathematical ideas that can be challenging for a developer whose background is in electronics or computer science. My experience has taught me to understand the concepts and behavior of an algorithm while relying on well-reviewed libraries for its implementation.

docs.title: Using cryptography without implementing every algorithm
docs.text:
PKI software needs cryptographic operations: generating keys, creating signatures, and checking certificates, among others. In practice, I usually use an established cryptographic library rather than implement the underlying algorithms myself.

That does not mean the mathematics is irrelevant. I need to understand what an algorithm is supposed to do, its inputs and outputs, and the properties that matter when using it. But understanding an algorithm at that level is different from being able to diagnose a subtle error in its mathematical implementation.

docs.title: Why comparing results matters
docs.text:
When a calculation produces an unexpected result, limited knowledge of the underlying mathematics can make the cause difficult to find. Is the issue in the algorithm, the input, the data format, or the way the operation was called?

One way I investigate is to compare the same operation against a trusted, independently implemented library. A difference gives me a starting point for checking the inputs, parameters, and output formats. A match is useful evidence, although it does not by itself prove that an implementation is secure or correct in every case.

docs.title: OpenSSL as a reference for PKI development
docs.text:
I often use OpenSSL as a reference when working with cryptographic operations. Its widely used implementation gives me a practical way to inspect data and compare results while developing PKI software.

Of course, no library is completely free of bugs. OpenSSL still needs appropriate configuration, maintenance, and security updates. For my work, its value is that it provides a well-established point of comparison when I am investigating an unexpected result.

docs.title: From learning to building tools
docs.text:
Working through these questions and checking results with OpenSSL led me to build several tools of my own. They help me inspect and experiment with the formats and operations used in PKI.

For me, developing cryptographic software is a continuing process of learning: understand the concepts, use established implementations carefully, and investigate differences rather than assuming the first result is correct.

Originally published in Korean on March 30, 2023: 암호학과 수학 그리고 OpenSSL에 관해.

docs.title: Why I Use OpenSSL and Qt to Build PKI Tools
docs.text: When I build public key infrastructure (PKI) tools, I use OpenSSL for cryptographic and PKI functionality and Qt for the user interface. They are not the only choices, but together they give me the capabilities and cross-platform support I need.

docs.title: Why OpenSSL for PKI development?
docs.text:
Of the PKI libraries I have personally used, OpenSSL has offered the broadest range of functionality. My experience does not cover every available library, but OpenSSL has been a useful foundation for working with cryptography and PKI data.

Its long history, wide use, and availability across platforms also make it a valuable reference when I need to investigate an operation or compare results. PKI relies heavily on standards, and being able to compare behavior with an established implementation helps me understand interoperability problems.

docs.title: When I use mbed TLS
docs.text: For smaller projects, I have also used mbed TLS. I have found it a capable cryptographic library, but in my experience it has offered less of the broad PKI functionality I need for tools that work with complex ASN.1 formats and protocols such as OCSP, TSP, and CMP. The right choice depends on the version and the requirements of the project.

docs.title: The trade-off: OpenSSL can be complex
docs.text:
OpenSSL's breadth comes with a learning curve. I have found parts of its code difficult to follow, and some internal APIs less thoroughly documented than I would like. ASN.1 handling also makes extensive use of macros. Understanding a large library takes time, especially when working beyond its public interfaces.

For licensing, check the license for the specific OpenSSL release and all dependencies before distribution. OpenSSL 3.0 and later use the Apache License 2.0; older releases have different terms. OpenSSL licensing

docs.title: Why Qt for cross-platform user interfaces?
docs.text:
I use Qt because it makes user interface development approachable and supports desktop platforms beyond Windows. Earlier in my development work, I used MFC with Visual Studio and focused on Windows. With Qt, I found it easier to write and maintain code intended for Windows, macOS, and Linux.

Qt also supports mobile platforms, although I have not personally used it for iOS or Android development. Cross-platform support does not remove every platform-specific task: building, testing, packaging, and distribution still need attention on each target system.

docs.title: Building BerEditor, CertMan, and CryptokiMan
docs.text:
Using Qt made it easier for me to compile and port BerEditor, CertMan, and CryptokiMan to macOS and Linux. At the time I originally wrote this post, I distributed macOS builds alongside the Windows versions. Linux packaging was more complicated and I had not yet made a Linux release available; I hoped to share one when time allowed.

That is a snapshot of my experience in 2023, not a current release list. For availability, check the JKLab website.

docs.title: Choosing tools for your own project
docs.text:
OpenSSL and Qt suit the tools I build, but another combination may be better for a different application. Consider the cryptographic operations and protocols you need, the platforms you support, resource limits, maintenance effort, documentation, and applicable licenses.

Originally published in Korean on February 24, 2023: OpenSSL 과 QT로 개발 하는 이유는?.

docs.title: Public Key Infrastructure (PKI): Concepts
docs.text: The term PKI appears in many fields. After working with it for a long time, I have come to think of PKI as a component that supports many different systems. It is rarely used on its own, but it turns up in many places. This article offers a brief overview of the concept.

docs.title: 1. What is PKI?
docs.text:
Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) is a system of capabilities, policies, and services that uses public-key cryptography to support authentication of users and devices.

There is no single universally fixed list of PKI components. A typical PKI includes Certificate Authorities (CAs) and Registration Authorities (RAs), and uses certificates issued by a CA to authenticate users or devices. The certificate and its issuing authority distinguish PKI from a generic public-key cryptography system.

docs.title: 2. PKI components
docs.text: The diagram below shows common PKI components and their relationships.

docs.title: 2.1 Certificate Authority (CA)
docs.text:
• Issues and distributes certificates for entities such as other CAs and end entities.
  • Revokes certificates at the request of an RA or a user, according to the PKI's procedures.
  • Publishes Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs) in a public location, often a directory service (DS).

docs.title: 2.2 Registration Authority (RA)
docs.text:
• Identifies users and asks a CA to register them or issue certificates.
  • Can request certificate revocation and provide certificate status lookup services.

docs.title: 2.3 Directory Server (DS)
docs.text:
• Stores and publicly publishes certificates and CRLs so they can be retrieved by others.
  • Often uses LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol).
  • May also publish information through web or FTP services.

docs.title: 2.4 End Entity (EE)
docs.text:
• A user, device, or other subject that uses a certificate issued by a CA.
  • May create digital signatures or verify signatures, depending on its role.

docs.title: 3. Additional PKI services
docs.text: A PKI can operate with its core components, but additional services can provide useful security and status information.

docs.title: 3.1 Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP)
docs.text:
• CRLs are published periodically, so they may not reflect a certificate's status immediately.
  • A CRL can also be large and require significant network traffic. OCSP can return status information for an individual certificate.
  • OCSP is commonly used as an alternative or complement to retrieving a full CRL. The actual freshness of a response depends on the service and its configuration.

docs.title: 3.2 Time-Stamping Authority (TSA)
docs.text:
• A TSA provides trusted evidence that data existed at a particular time.
  • It responds to a time-stamp request with a signed token that binds a time to a digest of the submitted data.
  • Time-stamp services can also provide ordering information, such as a sequence number, when the service is designed to do so.

docs.title: 4. PKI use cases
docs.text: PKI supports many kinds of systems. Common examples include:

docs.title: 4.1 Web security
docs.text: • TLS certificates are used to authenticate servers in HTTPS connections and support secure communication.

docs.title: 4.2 Document encryption and signatures
docs.text: • Certificates can be used in workflows for encrypting documents such as PDFs and for creating or verifying digital signatures.

docs.title: 4.3 Email authentication and encryption
docs.text:
• S/MIME uses certificates for signing and encrypting email.
  • OpenPGP (often called PGP) is also based on public-key cryptography, but its key distribution and trust models are not inherently based on the X.509 certificate hierarchy used by many PKI systems.

docs.title: 4.4 User authentication
docs.text: • Certificate-based technologies are used for user authentication, including in some VPN deployments.

docs.title: 4.5 Online banking
docs.text: • In South Korea, PKI systems have been used in various online banking services to authenticate users.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
PKI brings together many technologies: each component and each certificate-related process has its own details. This article has covered only the basic concepts, as a starting point for understanding the wider system.

Tags: DS · EE · certificates · CA · RA · PKI · Public Key Infrastructure · End Entity

docs.title: A Story About Digital Signatures and Certificates
docs.text: Digital signatures and certificates are technical topics in public key infrastructure (PKI). Here is a plain-language explanation.

docs.title: The seal certificate analogy
docs.text:
A useful real-world analogy for a digital signature and a certificate is a certificate of registered seal. In a paper-based process, someone signs a document with a seal, and the certificate helps others confirm that the seal is valid and belongs to that person.

In the offline world, people handle identity checks and documents in person. As these processes move online, they are digitized: a person signs data with a private key, and another party verifies the signature with the corresponding public key. A certificate is a digitally signed document that vouches for the relationship between that public key and its subject.

The analogy is not exact, but it helps explain the roles. A seal is applied to a physical document. A digital signature is computed over digital data, so changing the data after signing causes signature verification to fail. In a paper process, people may compare a copy with the signed original to check whether the document was altered.

docs.title: Security needs when moving online
docs.text:
When paper-based processes move online, we need to consider several security properties:

  1. Confidentiality — Only authorized people should be able to read the document.
  2. Integrity — Changes to the digital data should be detectable.
  3. Authenticity — The recipient should be able to verify who signed the document.
  4. Non-repudiation — The signature can provide evidence that the holder of the signing key signed the data, making a later denial harder.

In an offline process, identity documents can help establish who is present; an envelope can limit who sees the contents; and comparing copies can reveal changes. A person also signs the document directly. Online, cryptography helps address these needs: digital signatures provide integrity checks and support signer authentication and non-repudiation, while encryption protects confidentiality.

docs.title: Why certificates matter
docs.text:
Anyone can generate a key pair for creating digital signatures. But how can a verifier know that a particular public key belongs to the person it claims to represent?

A trusted party must vouch for that association. The digitally signed statement that binds a public key to its subject is a certificate. A certificate does not prove that a document is safe or that every claim in it is true; it helps establish trust in the identity associated with a public key.

People can also own more than one physical seal. A certificate of registered seal helps distinguish the seal officially associated with a person. Digital certificates play a related role for public keys.

We trust a certificate of registered seal because it is issued by an authorized public institution. Digital certificates are issued by a Certificate Authority (CA), so trust in the CA matters. Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) is the set of policies, roles, systems, and processes that supports issuing, managing, and validating certificates and public keys.

docs.title: In summary
docs.text:
As society moves from offline processes to digital ones, we need security mechanisms suited to digital data. Encryption helps provide confidentiality, and digital signatures help protect integrity and establish the signer’s identity. PKI provides an infrastructure for trusting the public keys used in these online interactions.

Tags: certificates · CA · registered seals · PKI · digital signatures

docs.title: Private Keys, Public Keys, and Certificates
docs.text:
When you work with a PKI system, you often encounter three terms: private key, public key, and certificate. They are fundamental to digital signatures. Here is a simple explanation.

In short:

  • The private key creates a digital signature.
  • The public key verifies that signature.
  • A certificate vouches for the identity associated with a public key.

For an introduction to digital signatures and certificates, see Digital Signatures and Certificates.

docs.title: What is a private key?
docs.text:
A private key is used to create a digital signature. It must remain under the control of its owner and must not be shared with other people. Protecting the private key is one of the central security requirements of a PKI system.

Private keys are therefore often stored in encrypted form or protected by a more secure device, such as a Hardware Security Module (HSM).

docs.title: What is a public key?
docs.text:
A public key is used to verify a digital signature. The person who holds the private key creates the signature; anyone who needs to check the signed content can use the corresponding public key to verify it.

Signature verification normally uses both the signature and the original data. A digital signature by itself does not provide confidentiality. It lets a verifier check that the signed data has not changed and that the signature was made by someone with the corresponding private key.

As its name suggests, a public key is intended to be shared so others can verify signatures. Unlike a private key, it generally does not need to be kept secret.

docs.title: What is a certificate?
docs.text:
Anyone can generate a public and private key pair. That means anyone can create signatures and anyone can verify a signature if they have the corresponding public key. The remaining question is: whose public key is it?

A certificate helps answer that question. A Certificate Authority (CA) issues a certificate that binds a subject’s identity to a public key. The CA signs the certificate data with its private key. A verifier can use the CA’s public key to check that signature and determine whether the certificate was signed by that CA and whether its contents have been altered.

A CA typically issues certificates and makes them available through a public repository or other distribution service. Because a certificate contains the public key, people can obtain the key from the certificate and use it to verify signatures.

docs.title: In summary
docs.text:
The basic idea of signature verification in a PKI system is straightforward: the private key signs, and the public key verifies. Validating a certificate involves more steps. A verifier may need to build and validate a certificate path through intermediate CAs up to a trusted root, and check that the certificates are valid for the intended use. This process is called path validation.

Understanding these basic terms is a useful first step toward understanding the more complex parts of PKI.

Tags: certificates · public keys · private keys

docs.title: ASN.1 Basic Encoding Rules (BER): TLV and Encoding Examples
docs.text: Basic Encoding Rules (BER) define how to encode values described using ASN.1 (Abstract Syntax Notation One). This guide explains the tag-length-value (TLV) structure, identifiers, lengths, and common ASN.1 types with hexadecimal examples.

docs.title: The BER tag-length-value structure
docs.text:
A BER encoding consists of an identifier, a length, and contents:

+----------------+----------------+----------------+
| Tag            | Length         | Value          |
+----------------+----------------+----------------+
  • Tag, also called the identifier, identifies the class, form, and tag number.
  • Length specifies the number of content octets in a definite-length encoding, or indicates an indefinite-length encoding.
  • Value, also called the contents, contains the encoded data.

A constructed value can contain nested TLV encodings. For example, the value of an outer element can contain two encoded elements:

Outer tag | Outer length | Tag 1 | Length 1 | Value 1 | Tag 2 | Length 2 | Value 2
                         |<---------------- outer contents ---------------->|

docs.title: BER identifier encoding
docs.text:
The first identifier octet contains the tag class, the primitive/constructed bit, and either the tag number or an indication that more identifier octets follow. Bit 7 is the most significant bit in the diagrams below.

Bits:  7  6 | 5 | 4  3  2  1  0
      class | P/C | tag number

docs.title: Tag classes
docs.text: Bits 7–6 Class 00 Universal 01 Application 10 Context-specific 11 Private

docs.title: Primitive and constructed forms
docs.text:
Bit 5 indicates the form:

Bit 5 Form Meaning 0 Primitive The contents represent the value directly. 1 Constructed The contents contain encoded components.

docs.title: Tag number encoding
docs.text:
For tag numbers 0–30, bits 4–0 contain the tag number directly. For tag numbers 31 or greater, those bits are 11111, and subsequent octets encode the tag number in groups of seven bits, most significant group first. The high bit of each subsequent octet is 1 if another octet follows and 0 for the last octet.

For tag numbers 31–127, one subsequent octet is sufficient. Larger tag numbers require two or more subsequent octets.

docs.title: Identifier examples
docs.text:
Class and form Tag number Binary identifier Hexadecimal Universal, primitive 2 00000010 02 Private, constructed 13 11101101 ED Application, primitive 40 01011111 00101000 5F 28

For example, 5F 28 starts with application class (01), primitive form (0), and 11111, indicating a high tag number. The next octet ends in the seven-bit value 0101000, or 40 in decimal.

docs.title: BER length encoding
docs.text: BER supports definite-length and indefinite-length encodings. Definite length has short and long forms; both encode the number of content octets, excluding the identifier and length octets.

docs.title: Short form
docs.text:
The short form uses one octet. Its most significant bit is 0, and its remaining seven bits hold a content length from 0 to 127.

0 | length in 7 bits

For a content length of 5 octets, the length octet is 00000101, or 05 in hexadecimal.

docs.title: Long form
docs.text:
In the long form, the most significant bit of the first length octet is 1. The remaining seven bits specify the number of subsequent length octets. Those octets encode the content length as an unsigned binary integer, most significant octet first.

1 | number of length octets | length octet(s)

For a content length of 1,020 octets:

Binary: 10000010 00000011 11111100
Hex:    82       03       FC

82 indicates that two length octets follow; 03 FC represents 1,020 in decimal.

docs.title: Indefinite form
docs.text:
The indefinite form uses the length octet 80 and does not state the content length. Instead, an end-of-contents marker (00 00) terminates the contents:

Tag | 80 | Contents | 00 00

BER permits indefinite length for constructed encodings; primitive encodings use definite length. DER, a more restrictive set of encoding rules based on BER, does not permit indefinite lengths.

docs.title: BER encoding examples for ASN.1 types
docs.text: The following examples use hexadecimal octets. Unless stated otherwise, the examples use primitive encodings and definite lengths. BER can permit other valid encodings; these examples do not enumerate every alternative.

docs.title: BOOLEAN
docs.text:
A BOOLEAN has universal tag 01 and one content octet. 00 represents FALSE; any nonzero octet represents TRUE in BER. DER requires FF for TRUE.

TRUE:   01 01 FF
FALSE:  01 01 00
        tag length value

docs.title: INTEGER
docs.text:
An INTEGER has universal tag 02. Its contents use the minimum number of octets needed for a signed two's-complement value, most significant octet first. A leading 00 may be needed to keep a positive value positive; negative values use two's complement.

72:  02 01 48
-2:  02 01 FE

docs.title: BIT STRING
docs.text:
For a primitive BIT STRING, tag 03 is followed by the length and contents. The first content octet gives the number of unused bits in the final data octet. The data bits are packed into octets, with padding at the end if necessary.

Value:    '101100001001'B
Encoding: 03 03 04 B0 90
          │  │  │  └───── data: 10110000 10010000
          │  │  └──────── 4 unused bits in the last octet
          │  └─────────── 3 content octets
          └────────────── BIT STRING tag

docs.title: OCTET STRING and NULL
docs.text:
A primitive OCTET STRING uses tag 04; its contents are the octets of the value. NULL uses tag 05 and has no content octets.

'A24F'H:  04 02 A2 4F
NULL:     05 00

docs.title: Explicit and implicit tagging
docs.text:
An EXPLICIT tag wraps the complete encoding of the underlying value. An IMPLICIT tag replaces its identifier. In this example, [21] is context-specific and the underlying BOOLEAN is TRUE:

ExplicitPresent ::= [21] EXPLICIT BOOLEAN
ImplicitPresent ::= [21] IMPLICIT BOOLEAN

EXPLICIT: B5 03 01 01 FF
          └ outer ┘ └ BOOLEAN ┘
IMPLICIT: 95 01 FF

B5 is constructed because it wraps another TLV; 95 is primitive because it replaces the primitive BOOLEAN identifier. The original example treats [21] BOOLEAN as explicit; writing EXPLICIT makes that assumption clear regardless of the module's tagging default.

docs.title: SEQUENCE
docs.text:
A SEQUENCE encodes its components in their declared order. Its universal constructed identifier is 30.

PersonnelRecord ::= SEQUENCE {
  name     OCTET STRING,
  location INTEGER { homeOffice(0), fieldOffice(1), roving(2) },
  age      INTEGER OPTIONAL
}

rockStar1 PersonnelRecord ::= {
  name '626967'H, location roving, age 26
}

30 0B                SEQUENCE, 11 content octets
   04 03 62 69 67    name: '626967'H
   02 01 02          location: roving (2)
   02 01 1A          age: 26

docs.title: SEQUENCE OF
docs.text:
A SEQUENCE OF encodes an ordered collection of values of the same type. For { 10, 12, -2, 8 }:

30 0C          SEQUENCE OF, 12 content octets
   02 01 0A    10
   02 01 0C    12
   02 01 FE    -2
   02 01 08     8

docs.title: SET
docs.text:
A SET contains named components whose order is not significant in BER. The following example uses an implicitly tagged SET and context-specific implicit tags for its fields:

PersonnelSet ::= [0] IMPLICIT SET {
  name     [0] IMPLICIT OCTET STRING,
  location [1] IMPLICIT INTEGER { home(0), field(1), roving(2) } OPTIONAL,
  age      [2] IMPLICIT INTEGER OPTIONAL
}

For location home, name '44617679'H, and age 44, one BER encoding is:

A0 0C                   context-specific constructed [0], 12 content octets
   81 01 00             location: home (0)
   80 04 44 61 76 79    name: '44617679'H
   82 01 2C             age: 44

DER imposes additional ordering rules, so this BER example should not be assumed to be DER.

docs.title: CHOICE
docs.text:
A CHOICE represents one alternative; the chosen alternative's encoding identifies it. Here the selected r-and-d alternative is an implicitly tagged SEQUENCE:

Division ::= CHOICE {
  manufacturing [0] IMPLICIT SEQUENCE {
    plantID INTEGER, majorProduct OCTET STRING
  },
  r-and-d [1] IMPLICIT SEQUENCE {
    labID INTEGER, currentProject OCTET STRING
  }
}

currentAssignment Division ::= r-and-d : {
  labID 48, currentProject '44582D37'H
}

A1 09                   context-specific constructed [1], 9 content octets
   02 01 30             labID: 48
   04 04 44 58 2D 37    currentProject: '44582D37'H

The source illustration labels the outer length 0C; the two components shown occupy 9 octets, so the corrected length is 09.

docs.title: OBJECT IDENTIFIER
docs.text:
An OBJECT IDENTIFIER (OID) uses universal tag 06. Combine the first two arcs as 40 × first arc + second arc; encode that combined value and each remaining arc as a base-128 subidentifier, most significant group first. Each octet's high bit is 1 if another octet of the same subidentifier follows and 0 on the last octet. The combined first subidentifier can itself require more than one octet.

For OID 1.0.8571.2.1:

06 05 28 C2 7B 02 01
      │  └───┘ │  └── arc 1
      │   8571 └───── arc 2
      └────────────── 40 × 1 + 0 = 40 (28 hex)

C2 7B represents 66 × 128 + 123 = 8571; its first high bit indicates continuation.

docs.title: GeneralizedTime and UTCTime
docs.text:
These types encode their textual time representations as character octets. For example, the character 1 is 31 and the decimal point is 2E in hexadecimal.

GeneralizedTime "19960415203000.0":
18 10 31 39 39 36 30 34 31 35 32 30 33 30 30 30 2E 30

UTCTime "9604152030Z":
17 0B 39 36 30 34 31 35 32 30 33 30 5A

These are BER examples. DER and specific profiles can impose stricter requirements on time representations.

docs.text: Adapted from the Korean series: Basic Encoding Rules (1/3), part 2, and part 3.

docs.title: ASN.1 BER vs DER: Differences and Encoding Examples
docs.text:
BER (Basic Encoding Rules) and DER (Distinguished Encoding Rules) specify how to encode ASN.1 values as bytes. BER allows multiple valid encodings for some values. DER adds restrictions to BER so that a given value, under a given ASN.1 type and schema, has a canonical encoding. Consequently, every valid DER encoding is also valid BER, but not every valid BER encoding is valid DER.

This guide compares the rules with hexadecimal examples and explains why DER matters for X.509 certificates and digital signatures. Both sets of rules are specified in ITU-T X.690.

docs.title: ASN.1, BER, and DER at a glance
docs.text:
ASN.1 (Abstract Syntax Notation One) describes data types and structures independently of their encoded form. Encoding rules specify how an ASN.1 value is represented as bytes for storage or transfer.

Feature BER DER Purpose Flexible encoding of ASN.1 values Canonical encoding with additional restrictions Encodings for a value Some values have multiple valid encodings One canonical encoding for a given value and type Length Definite, or indefinite for constructed encodings Definite, using the shortest permitted form Boolean TRUE Any nonzero contents octet Contents octet must be FF String encoding Some string types allow primitive or constructed forms String types covered below use primitive form SET and SET OF Component order can vary within BER rules Canonical ordering rules apply Typical use Protocols and applications that allow BER X.509 certificates and other formats requiring canonical bytes

The applicable protocol or file format determines which rules to use. DER is useful when a standard requires reproducible bytes; BER is useful when its flexibility is allowed.

docs.title: How ASN.1 tag-length-value encoding works
docs.text:
BER and DER encodings generally follow a tag-length-value (TLV) structure:

Tag       Length    Contents
01        01        FF

In this example, 01 is the universal tag for BOOLEAN, the next 01 says the contents are one octet long, and FF represents TRUE. A tag or length can occupy more than one octet. For constructed values, the contents contain encodings of component values.

docs.title: Boolean values: flexible BER versus canonical DER
docs.text:
A BOOLEAN has exactly one contents octet. Under BER, 00 means FALSE and any nonzero octet means TRUE. DER requires FF for TRUE:

01 01 00    FALSE: valid BER and DER
01 01 01    TRUE:  valid BER, but not DER
01 01 FF    TRUE:  valid BER and DER

The two TRUE encodings represent the same ASN.1 value but differ in bytes. DER removes that choice.

docs.title: Length encoding: definite and indefinite forms
Definite length
docs.text:
A definite length specifies the number of contents octets before the contents. For lengths from 0 through 127, the short form uses one length octet:

04 03 41 42 43
│  │  └─────── Contents: ASCII bytes for ABC
│  └────────── Length: 3 octets
└───────────── OCTET STRING tag

For larger lengths, the long form uses an initial octet indicating how many subsequent octets encode the length. For example, 81 80 specifies a contents length of 128 octets.

BER permits long-form lengths even where the short form would suffice. DER requires the shortest permitted length form:

04 03    41 42 43    OCTET STRING "ABC": valid BER and DER
04 81 03 41 42 43    OCTET STRING "ABC": valid BER, but not DER

docs.title: Indefinite length
docs.text:
BER also permits an indefinite length for constructed encodings. The length octet is 80, and an end-of-contents marker, 00 00, terminates the contents:

30 80             SEQUENCE, indefinite length
   02 01 05       INTEGER 5
00 00             End-of-contents marker

This is valid BER but not DER. A DER encoding of the same sequence uses a definite length:

30 03             SEQUENCE, 3 contents octets
   02 01 05       INTEGER 5

Indefinite length can be useful when encoding constructed data incrementally. It is not permitted for primitive values, and DER does not permit it for any value.

docs.title: Primitive and constructed string encodings
docs.text:
BER allows certain string types, including OCTET STRING, to use either primitive encoding or constructed encoding made of segments. Consider the octets for ABC:

04 03 41 42 43                  Primitive OCTET STRING: BER and DER

24 80                           Constructed OCTET STRING: BER only
   04 02 41 42                  Segment: AB
   04 01 43                     Segment: C
00 00                           End-of-contents marker

The constructed example is valid BER, but not DER. DER requires the primitive form for OCTET STRING and BIT STRING, as well as the other restricted character string types covered by X.690. Constructed encoding itself is not forbidden in DER: types such as SEQUENCE and SET are constructed.

docs.title: SET ordering and default values
docs.text:
DER adds rules beyond Boolean values and lengths:

  • SET: Components are encoded in the canonical order specified by their tags.
  • SET OF: Encoded elements are sorted according to the ordering rules for their complete encodings. This is distinct from the SET rule.
  • DEFAULT components: A component whose value equals its ASN.1 default must be omitted in DER. BER permits it to be encoded explicitly.

For example, with Example ::= SEQUENCE { flag BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE }, both examples below are valid BER encodings of the default-valued sequence, but only the first is DER:

30 00                Empty SEQUENCE: default applies; BER and DER
30 03 01 01 00       Explicit FALSE: BER, not DER

The schema is essential to interpreting a default value; the bytes alone do not identify the ASN.1 definition.

docs.title: INTEGER encoding: a rule BER already enforces
docs.text:
Not every constraint is unique to DER. BER already requires an INTEGER to use the minimum number of contents octets needed for its signed two's-complement value. For example:

02 01 7F       INTEGER 127: valid BER and DER
02 02 00 80    INTEGER 128: valid BER and DER; 00 keeps it positive
02 02 00 7F    INTEGER 127: invalid BER and DER; 00 is redundant

An extra leading octet is therefore not a valid way to illustrate a BER-versus-DER difference for an INTEGER.

docs.title: Why DER matters for X.509 certificates and digital signatures
docs.text:
A digital signature is calculated over bytes. If two encodings represent the same logical value but differ byte for byte, their hashes can differ too. Canonical DER encoding provides a consistent representation when a specification requires one.

For example, RFC 5280 specifies DER encoding of tbsCertificate for X.509 certificate signature calculation. A verifier must follow the relevant protocol and verify the exact signed data according to its rules; simply decoding and re-encoding arbitrary input does not make it valid DER or guarantee the correct verification result.

docs.title: BER, DER, and PEM: what is the difference?
docs.text:
BER and DER are ASN.1 encoding rules. PEM is a text format commonly used to carry Base64-encoded binary data between labeled boundary lines. A PEM certificate typically contains DER-encoded X.509 data:

-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----
...Base64-encoded certificate bytes...
-----END CERTIFICATE-----

A file extension alone does not reliably identify the encoding. Check the file contents and the format expected by the application.

docs.title: How to inspect BER and DER data
docs.text:
Download BerEditor to inspect and edit ASN.1 BER/DER data. When comparing an encoding with DER requirements, check its length forms, primitive or constructed representation, ordering, default values, and any type-specific constraints. A BER parser accepting a file does not by itself prove that the file is DER-compliant.

For related concepts, see Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) Concepts and Private Keys, Public Keys, and Certificates.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• ITU-T X.690: BER, CER, and DER encoding rules
  • RFC 5280: Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure Certificate and CRL Profile

docs.title: Certificate and CMS File Extensions: PEM, DER, PFX, P7B, P7M and P7S
docs.text:
When working with certificates and private keys, you will encounter extensions such as .pem, .der, .crt, .cer, .csr, .pfx, .p12, .key, .p7b, .p7m, and .p7s. They are useful hints, but a filename extension alone does not reliably tell you what a file contains or how it is encoded.

The key distinction is between the object—such as a certificate, private key, or certificate signing request—and its encoding or container. A certificate, for example, can be stored as binary DER or as PEM text.

docs.title: Certificate and key file formats at a glance
docs.text: Extension Common use What to check .pem PEM-encoded certificate, key, request, or other object Read the BEGIN and END labels; one file can contain multiple blocks. .der Binary DER-encoded ASN.1 object Determine whether it is a certificate, key, or another object. .crt, .cer Certificate Either can contain PEM text or binary DER; verify the actual content. .csr Certificate signing request Usually a PKCS #10 request in PEM or DER; it is not an issued certificate. .pfx, .p12 PKCS #12 container May contain a private key, certificates, and additional certificates; contents vary. .key Usually a private key May be PEM or DER, encrypted or unencrypted. .p7b, .p7c PKCS #7 certificate collection Can contain certificates and CRLs; inspect the actual structure and encoding. .p7m, .p7s, .p7z CMS / S/MIME message, signature, or compressed data The suffix is a hint; check the MIME type, CMS content type, and encoding.

docs.title: What is PEM?
docs.text:
PEM is a text representation commonly used for PKI objects. A PEM block has a Base64-encoded body between labeled boundary lines. The label identifies the kind of object inside. The encoding itself provides no confidentiality: Base64 is not encryption. RFC 7468

A PEM certificate looks like this:

-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----
... Base64-encoded certificate data ...
-----END CERTIFICATE-----

A PEM file can also contain multiple blocks, such as a certificate followed by intermediate certificates. Applications differ in which objects and ordering they accept.

docs.title: PEM private key labels
docs.text:
You may see several labels:

-----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----
-----BEGIN ENCRYPTED PRIVATE KEY-----
-----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----

PRIVATE KEY commonly denotes an unencrypted PKCS #8 private-key structure, while ENCRYPTED PRIVATE KEY denotes an encrypted PKCS #8 structure. RSA PRIVATE KEY identifies a traditional RSA-specific structure; some older encrypted PEM files also contain Proc-Type and DEK-Info headers. Do not assume a key is encrypted just because it is in PEM format. Keep private keys confidential regardless of extension.

docs.title: What is DER?
docs.text:
DER (Distinguished Encoding Rules) is a binary ASN.1 encoding. A DER-encoded certificate is not normally readable in a text editor; use a certificate or ASN.1 viewer to inspect it. DER can encode objects besides certificates, so a .der extension does not identify the object type by itself.

PEM commonly wraps an encoded ASN.1 object in labeled Base64 text. Converting a certificate between PEM and DER changes its representation; it does not create a new certificate or change its validity period.

docs.title: CRT and CER: certificate extensions
docs.text:
.crt and .cer usually indicate certificate files. Both extensions can be used for PEM or DER encoding; conventions differ across tools and platforms. Check the contents or use a certificate inspection tool instead of assuming the encoding from the suffix.

A PEM file starts with a visible -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE----- line. A DER certificate is binary. A .crt or .cer file can also contain something unexpected, so successful parsing matters more than its name.

docs.title: CSR: certificate signing request
docs.text:
A certificate signing request (CSR) asks a certificate authority to issue a certificate. A PKCS #10 CSR contains a public key and requested subject information, and is signed using the corresponding private key. It can also contain requested attributes or extensions; the CA decides what to include in the issued certificate.

A CSR is not a certificate and should not contain the private key. A common PEM label is:

-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE REQUEST-----
... Base64-encoded request data ...
-----END CERTIFICATE REQUEST-----

Older tools may use NEW CERTIFICATE REQUEST. RFC 7468 specifies the CERTIFICATE REQUEST label for conforming generators and allows parsers to recognize the older label. RFC 7468 §7

docs.title: PFX and P12: PKCS #12 containers
docs.text:
.pfx and .p12 commonly refer to PKCS #12 files. A PKCS #12 container can package a private key and its certificate with additional certificates, making it useful for importing or exporting an identity. The exact contents depend on how the file was created. RFC 7292

PKCS #12 supports password-based protection, but protection depends on how the file was created and which algorithms and password were used. Treat a container that might hold a private key as sensitive; use a strong password where applicable and transfer it securely.

docs.title: PKCS #7 and CMS: certificate collections and secure messages
docs.text:
PKCS #7 describes a syntax for cryptographic messages. CMS (Cryptographic Message Syntax) builds on PKCS #7 and defines structures such as SignedData and EnvelopedData; CMS and older PKCS #7 formats are related but are not interchangeable in every case. CMS is used by S/MIME and other applications for signed, encrypted, or other protected content. RFC 5652

Common extensions include:

Extension Typical use .p7b A PKCS #7 certificate bundle, often containing one or more certificates and possibly CRLs. Microsoft: certificate export .p7c An S/MIME certificates-only message, represented as a degenerate SignedData structure. .p7m An S/MIME CMS message, such as attached signed data or enveloped encrypted data. The extension alone does not say which. .p7s An S/MIME detached signature; verification also requires the original signed MIME content. .p7z S/MIME compressed data.

The S/MIME names above are conventions specified in RFC 8551. Other applications may use different names. A .p7b certificate bundle generally does not include a private key; PKCS #12 is commonly used when an identity with its private key must be transferred. Neither an extension nor a certificate bundle establishes trust.

A PKCS #7 or CMS object can be encoded as binary ASN.1 or represented as labeled PEM text; a complete S/MIME message is MIME formatted and can include a Base64 transfer-encoded attachment. The extension by itself does not identify which representation you have. CMS also permits BER encoding, including forms that are not DER.

docs.title: KEY: a private key file
docs.text: A .key extension generally indicates a private key, but it does not establish whether the file is PEM or DER, which key algorithm it uses, or whether it is encrypted. Inspect it with a suitable tool and avoid copying its contents into tickets, logs, or public repositories.

docs.title: How to inspect certificate files with OpenSSL
docs.text:
These examples assume the named file contains the indicated object. They display information without changing the original file.

# Inspect a PEM certificate
openssl x509 -in certificate.pem -inform PEM -noout -text

# Inspect a DER certificate
openssl x509 -in certificate.der -inform DER -noout -text

# Inspect a PEM certificate signing request
openssl req -in request.csr -inform PEM -noout -text -verify

# Inspect a PKCS #12 container without outputting its keys or certificates
openssl pkcs12 -in identity.p12 -info -noout

# Print a binary DER CMS structure without verifying its signature
openssl cms -cmsout -print -noout -inform DER -in message.p7m

# Print certificates from a DER-encoded PKCS #7 certificate bundle
openssl pkcs7 -print_certs -inform DER -in certificates.p7b -noout

For PEM-encoded PKCS #7 or CMS input, use -inform PEM; for a complete MIME-formatted S/MIME message, the CMS command supports -inform SMIME. Parsing a CMS structure or printing certificates does not verify signatures, certificate chains, or trust. Detached signature verification also needs the exact signed content. See the OpenSSL cms and pkcs7 documentation.

The PKCS #12 command may prompt for a password. A verification result for a CSR checks its signature; it does not mean a CA has issued or approved a certificate. If a command fails, check the object type, encoding, password, and OpenSSL version. See the OpenSSL documentation for x509, req, and pkcs12.

docs.title: Convert a certificate between PEM and DER
docs.text:
# PEM to DER
openssl x509 -in certificate.pem -inform PEM -out certificate.der -outform DER

# DER to PEM
openssl x509 -in certificate.der -inform DER -out certificate.pem -outform PEM

Choose output filenames that do not overwrite files you need. These commands are for certificates; use the appropriate command for keys or requests.

docs.title: Is a .crt file always PEM?
docs.text: No. A .crt certificate can be PEM or DER. Check its contents or parse it with the appropriate input format.

docs.title: Are .pfx and .p12 different formats?
docs.text: Both are commonly used for PKCS #12 containers. Their extensions alone do not reveal the contents, password protection, or algorithms used.

docs.title: Is a .p7m file always encrypted?
docs.text: No. It can contain signed data, encrypted enveloped data, or another S/MIME content type. Inspect its MIME and CMS structure.

docs.title: Is a PEM private key secure because it is Base64 encoded?
docs.text: No. Base64 is an encoding, not encryption. Use appropriate key protection and restrict access to the file.

docs.title: Post-Quantum Cryptography Algorithms: A Guide to PQC
docs.text:
Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) uses cryptographic algorithms designed to remain secure against attacks by both classical and sufficiently capable quantum computers. PQC runs on conventional computers; it does not require a quantum network or quantum computer.

The first NIST PQC standards specify ML-KEM for establishing shared keys and ML-DSA and SLH-DSA for digital signatures. This guide explains their roles, differences, and practical implications for TLS, certificates, and PKI. Standards information is current as of November 22, 2026. NIST: PQC standards

docs.title: Why is post-quantum cryptography needed?
docs.text:
A sufficiently powerful, fault-tolerant quantum computer could run Shor's algorithm to break the mathematical problems underlying RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography. That threatens commonly deployed public-key encryption, key agreement, and digital signatures. Such a machine is not assumed to be available today, and its arrival date is uncertain. NIST: Post-Quantum Cryptography

A concern is harvest now, decrypt later: an adversary can record encrypted traffic today and attempt to decrypt it in the future. Information that must remain confidential for many years may therefore need quantum-resistant key establishment before a large quantum computer exists. Digital signatures have different lifecycle considerations, including the need to verify long-lived signatures and protect signing keys.

PQC primarily replaces vulnerable public-key mechanisms. Symmetric encryption and hash functions are affected differently by quantum algorithms; they do not all become unusable, and parameter choices and applications still matter. PQC is not the same as quantum key distribution (QKD).

docs.title: NIST post-quantum algorithm overview
docs.text:
Algorithm Standard Purpose Main mathematical approach Parameter sets ML-KEM FIPS 203 Establish a shared secret Module lattices ML-KEM-512, ML-KEM-768, ML-KEM-1024 ML-DSA FIPS 204 Digital signatures Module lattices ML-DSA-44, ML-DSA-65, ML-DSA-87 SLH-DSA FIPS 205 Digital signatures Stateless hash-based signatures SHA-2 and SHAKE variants across security and size/speed choices

NIST published all three standards in August 2024. Their parameter-set names are identifiers; they should not be read as interchangeable security-bit counts. Security, performance, public-key size, signature size, and ecosystem support vary by parameter set. Consult the standards and deployment profile when selecting one.

docs.title: ML-KEM: post-quantum key establishment
docs.text:
ML-KEM (Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism), derived from CRYSTALS-Kyber, establishes a shared secret across a public channel. It is a key encapsulation mechanism (KEM), not a digital signature algorithm or a general-purpose file encryption format. FIPS 203

A simplified exchange works as follows:

  1. The recipient generates an ML-KEM public key and private key, and makes the public key available.
  2. The sender encapsulates to the recipient's public key, producing a ciphertext and a shared secret.
  3. The sender sends the ciphertext to the recipient.
  4. The recipient decapsulates the ciphertext with the private key to obtain the same shared secret.
  5. A protocol derives appropriate symmetric keys from that secret and uses authenticated encryption to protect data.

The public key must be authenticated by the surrounding protocol; ML-KEM alone does not establish who owns it. A secure protocol must also handle key derivation, algorithm negotiation, and failure behavior correctly. NIST SP 800-227: Recommendations for KEMs

NIST IR 8547 recommends ML-KEM-768 as a default parameter set, while recognizing that other sets can be appropriate for particular requirements. This is NIST guidance, not a guarantee of compatibility with every product or policy. NIST IR 8547

docs.title: ML-DSA: lattice-based digital signatures
docs.text:
ML-DSA (Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm), derived from CRYSTALS-Dilithium, signs messages with a private key and verifies signatures with the corresponding public key. A successful verification provides evidence of integrity and of possession of the signing key; identity depends on how the public key is authenticated. FIPS 204

ML-DSA is intended for signature use cases such as software signing and PKI, subject to the relevant profile and implementation support. The three standardized parameter sets offer different security and performance trade-offs. A digital signature does not encrypt the message or establish a shared secret.

docs.title: SLH-DSA: stateless hash-based digital signatures
docs.text:
SLH-DSA (Stateless Hash-Based Digital Signature Algorithm), derived from SPHINCS+, is a signature scheme based on hash-function security. Its different mathematical foundation provides an alternative to lattice-based signatures. It is called stateless because signing does not require maintaining the per-signature state required by stateful hash-based schemes. FIPS 205

SLH-DSA has parameter sets using SHA-2 or SHAKE, with s variants favoring smaller signatures and f variants favoring faster signing. Signature sizes and signing performance can differ substantially from ML-DSA; benchmark the specific parameter set and workload before deployment.

docs.title: Other algorithms and standards in development
docs.text:
• FALCON / FN-DSA: NIST selected FALCON for standardization as a lattice-based signature scheme. FIPS 206 remains in development in NIST's published project status. Check the current standard before deployment. NIST PQC standardization
  • HQC: NIST selected this code-based KEM for standardization in 2025 as an alternative with a different mathematical foundation from ML-KEM. Selection is not the same as a final published FIPS standard. NIST: HQC selection

Additional signature candidates continue to be evaluated. Check NIST's current publications and applicable protocol profiles rather than assuming a candidate is standardized or interoperable.

docs.title: PQC, TLS, and X.509 certificates
docs.text:
TLS uses several cryptographic functions with different roles: key establishment protects the session's derived keys; certificate signatures authenticate the certificate chain; and handshake signatures authenticate the server or client. Replacing one role with a PQC algorithm does not automatically replace the others.

For example, using post-quantum key establishment in a TLS connection does not by itself mean that its X.509 certificates use post-quantum signatures. A complete migration must account for clients, servers, TLS libraries, certificate authorities, HSMs, certificate profiles, monitoring, and other relying parties. Whether a particular algorithm or combination is supported depends on the protocol standard and the products in use.

Hybrid key establishment combines a classical mechanism and a post-quantum mechanism in a specified construction. It can provide a transition path, but its security and interoperability depend on the actual protocol and implementation. Use an established, reviewed profile rather than inventing a combination. Hybrid key establishment and hybrid signatures solve different problems. NIST IR 8547

docs.title: How to plan a post-quantum migration
docs.text:
1. Inventory cryptography. Find RSA, Diffie–Hellman, ECDH, ECDSA, and other public-key uses across applications, certificates, protocols, HSMs, and suppliers. Record algorithm and parameter choices, dependencies, and certificate lifetimes.
  2. Prioritize long-lived data and high-impact systems. Consider confidentiality lifetime, harvest-now-decrypt-later exposure, signed data retention, and the time needed to replace difficult-to-update systems.
  3. Identify dependencies and standards. Check CA, operating system, browser, library, hardware, and protocol support, along with applicable regulatory and sector requirements.
  4. Test interoperability and performance. Measure handshake sizes, bandwidth, memory, CPU, signature and key sizes, certificate chains, and operational limits with real workloads.
  5. Build crypto agility. Support controlled algorithm and key rotation, inventory updates, monitoring, and rollback. Avoid hard-coding assumptions about key or signature sizes.
  6. Deploy in stages and monitor. Use supported, reviewed implementations and protocol profiles. Test renewal, recovery, revocation, logging, and fallback behavior before wider rollout.

NIST's final IR 8547 transition report describes its approach to moving away from quantum-vulnerable algorithms. Its timelines apply within NIST standards and guidelines and should not be treated as a universal legal deadline for every organization. Applicable requirements can depend on jurisdiction, sector, and system classification.

docs.title: Is PQC the same as quantum cryptography?
docs.text: No. PQC algorithms run on classical computers and are designed to resist quantum and classical attacks. Quantum cryptography, including QKD, uses quantum physical phenomena and has different infrastructure and security assumptions.

docs.title: Does PQC replace AES and SHA-2?
docs.text: PQC standards primarily address public-key key establishment and digital signatures. AES and SHA-2 have different quantum security considerations; the right key size, hash function, and protocol still depend on the application and policy.

docs.title: Which PQC algorithm replaces RSA?
docs.text: There is no single drop-in replacement for every RSA use. ML-KEM addresses key establishment, while ML-DSA and SLH-DSA address signatures. The applicable protocol must support the chosen algorithm and its encoding.

docs.title: Is ML-KEM encryption?
docs.text: ML-KEM establishes a shared secret; it does not directly encrypt arbitrary application data. Protocols use the secret to derive symmetric keys for authenticated encryption.

docs.title: Are post-quantum algorithms guaranteed to be secure forever?
docs.text: No. Their security depends on mathematical assumptions, correct implementations, secure key management, and continued cryptanalysis. Follow standards updates and plan for algorithm agility.

docs.text:

  • NIST IR 8547: Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography Standards.

docs.title: TLS and SSL Certificate Validity Periods: Policy and 2026–2029 Timeline
docs.text:
Publicly trusted TLS server certificates issued from March 15, 2026 have a maximum validity of 200 days. That limit falls to 100 days on March 15, 2027 and 47 days on March 15, 2029. These are maximums: a certificate authority (CA) can issue a certificate for a shorter period. The rules apply according to the certificate's issuance date. CA/Browser Forum, TLS Baseline Requirements §6.3.2

This guide describes the CA/Browser Forum's policy for publicly trusted TLS server certificates, commonly called SSL certificates. It is current as of November 22, 2026. Private PKI certificates, client certificates, code-signing certificates, and CA certificates have different applicable policies; do not assume this schedule governs them.

docs.title: Public TLS certificate maximum validity timeline
docs.text:
Certificate issuance date Maximum validity Before March 15, 2026 398 days March 15, 2026 through March 14, 2027 200 days March 15, 2027 through March 14, 2029 100 days On or after March 15, 2029 47 days

The limits are specified in §6.3.2 of the TLS Baseline Requirements. For example, a certificate issued on March 14, 2027 falls under the 200-day limit; one issued on March 15 falls under the 100-day limit. A policy change does not, by itself, shorten the validity dates already encoded in an existing certificate. Existing certificates must still satisfy the rules applicable to their issuance and remain subject to revocation and relying-party policies.

The requirements calculate a day as 86,400 seconds, and any extra time counts as another day. They also recommend a one-day margin: for example, certificates issued in the 200-day period should not exceed 199 days by default. The mandatory maximum and recommended margin are distinct. Check the CA's actual certificate lifetime rather than assuming every CA issues for the maximum.

docs.title: What is a TLS certificate validity period?
docs.text:
An X.509 certificate contains notBefore and notAfter timestamps. Its validity period is the interval between them. A relying party checks the time as part of certificate validation, along with other requirements such as the hostname, chain of trust, and applicable policies. A valid date alone does not guarantee trust. RFC 5280 §4.1.2.5

A renewed certificate is a newly issued certificate with its own validity period. Buying a multi-year service subscription does not extend an individual public TLS certificate beyond the applicable limit: the service must issue and deploy replacement certificates during the subscription.

docs.title: Domain validation reuse is a separate limit
docs.text:
Before issuing a public TLS certificate, a CA must validate authorization for the domain names or IP addresses. The CA/Browser Forum separately limits how long the CA may reuse eligible validation data or a completed validation. These limits are measured before issuance, not from the certificate's expiration date. TLS Baseline Requirements §4.2.1

Certificate issuance date Maximum domain/IP validation reuse Before March 15, 2026 398 days March 15, 2026 through March 14, 2027 200 days March 15, 2027 through March 14, 2029 100 days On or after March 15, 2029 10 days

From March 15, 2026, the maximum reuse period for subject identity information validation is 398 days under the same section. Individual validation methods have additional conditions, and a CA may use shorter periods. In particular, 10 days is not the certificate lifetime: it is the future maximum reuse window for eligible domain/IP validation information. A certificate issued after March 15, 2029 can have a validity period of up to 47 days.

docs.title: Why are certificate lifetimes getting shorter?
docs.text:
Shorter lifetimes limit the time a misissued certificate or compromised key can remain usable before the certificate expires. They also encourage automated issuance and replacement. Expiration is not a substitute for revocation: a compromised or incorrectly issued certificate may need to be revoked promptly. Let's Encrypt: Certificate Lifetime Rationale and Plans

The trade-off is operational: certificates must be replaced more often, so failed validation, inaccessible challenge endpoints, deployment errors, or missed reloads can cause outages unless the lifecycle is monitored.

docs.title: How to prepare for shorter TLS certificate lifetimes
docs.text:
1. Inventory certificates and endpoints. Include load balancers, reverse proxies, CDNs, APIs, mail servers, appliances, and internal deployment targets that use public certificates.
  2. Automate issuance and deployment. Use an ACME client or your CA's supported automation. Ensure that the certificate and corresponding private key reach every endpoint and that services reload them safely. RFC 8555: ACME
  3. Automate validation. Check that the chosen domain-control challenge can be completed on every renewal, including any DNS or network permissions it needs. Wildcard certificates require an appropriate validation method, such as DNS-01.
  4. Renew early and monitor the deployed certificate. Allow time for retries and alert on renewal failures, imminent expiration, and certificates that were issued but not deployed. Verify each externally reachable endpoint, not just the CA's issuance dashboard.
  5. Test failure recovery. Exercise DNS changes, CA access failures, credential rotation, deployment rollback, and certificate reloads. Keep challenge credentials and private keys protected.
  6. Check vendor and CA policies. Devices that require manual import, strict change windows, or proprietary APIs may need replacement or a different deployment workflow before the 47-day limit takes effect.

ACME Renewal Information (ARI) lets a CA suggest a renewal window to compatible clients; it can help spread renewal load and respond to CA guidance. Consult the CA and client documentation for support. RFC 9773

docs.title: Example: Let's Encrypt's schedule
docs.text: As of its July 2026 documentation, Let's Encrypt's default certificates have a 90-day lifetime; it also offers shorter profiles. Its published plan moves the default to 64 days on February 10, 2027 and then 45 days on February 16, 2028. These are that CA's planned lifetimes, not the industry-wide maximums. Confirm the current plan and the profile used by your ACME client before making changes. Let's Encrypt: Upcoming Features, 64-Day Certificate Lifetimes

docs.title: Are SSL certificates limited to 47 days now?
docs.text: No. As of November 22, 2026, the CA/Browser Forum maximum for newly issued publicly trusted TLS server certificates is 200 days. The 47-day maximum is scheduled for certificates issued on or after March 15, 2029. A CA may already offer a shorter lifetime.

docs.title: Does a 47-day certificate require domain validation every 47 days?
docs.text: Not necessarily. The validation reuse limit and the certificate validity limit are different. From March 15, 2029, the maximum reuse window for eligible domain/IP validation is 10 days before issuance. A CA may validate again sooner or apply method-specific requirements.

docs.title: Can a private CA issue certificates with longer lifetimes?
docs.text: The public TLS Baseline Requirements describe publicly trusted TLS server certificates; they do not automatically set the same limit for a separately trusted private PKI. Private certificates are still governed by their own CA policy, software, platform, and organizational requirements.

docs.title: How can I check a certificate's dates?
docs.text:
For a local PEM certificate, use OpenSSL:

openssl x509 -in certificate.pem -noout -subject -issuer -dates

To inspect the leaf certificate presented by a server, use the correct hostname for both connection and SNI:

openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com </dev/null 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer -dates

Replace example.com with your hostname. This displays the presented certificate's dates; it is not a complete certificate validation or an inventory of every backend.
